prompt: At its simplest, what does mass spectrometry measure?

choices.text: The mass (molecular weight) of a molecule
The wavelengths of light that a molecule absorbs
choices.why: That describes absorption spectroscopy. Mass spectrometry measures the masses of molecules and their fragments.

choices.text: The bond angles and bond lengths in a molecule
choices.why: Mass spectrometry gives masses, not bond angles or lengths. Structural clues come from the masses of the fragments.

choices.text: The number of electrons shared in each bond
choices.why: Mass spectrometry sorts and counts ions by mass; it doesn't count bonding electrons.

explanation: At its simplest, mass spectrometry (MS) measures the mass, and therefore the molecular weight (MW), of a molecule. It often gives structural information too, from the masses of the fragments produced when molecules break apart.

prompt: What three basic parts do all mass spectrometers have?

choices.text: An ionization source, a mass analyzer and a detector
A light source, a sample cell and a detector
choices.why: That is the layout of an instrument that measures absorbed light. A mass spectrometer charges molecules, sorts the ions and counts them.

choices.text: A magnet, a quadrupole and a detector
choices.why: A magnetic sector and a quadrupole are two different kinds of mass analyzer, and the list is missing the ionization source.

choices.text: A mass analyzer, a detector and a spectral database
choices.why: A database can help identify a spectrum, but it isn't one of the basic parts. The first part is the ionization source, which charges the molecules.

explanation: More than 20 kinds of commercial mass spectrometers exist, but all have three basic parts: an ionization source that gives sample molecules an electrical charge, a mass analyzer that separates ions by their mass-to-charge ratio, and a detector that observes and counts the separated ions.

prompt: What is the job of the mass analyzer in a mass spectrometer?

choices.text: It separates ions by their mass-to-charge ratio
It gives the sample molecules an electrical charge
choices.why: That is the job of the ionization source.

choices.text: It observes and counts the separated ions
choices.why: That is the job of the detector.

choices.text: It vaporizes the sample before ionization
choices.why: The sample is vaporized into the ionization source. The analyzer's job is to sort the ions by m/z.

explanation: The mass analyzer separates ions according to their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z). The ionization source charges the molecules, and the detector observes and counts the separated ions.

prompt: In an electron-impact instrument, the energy of the electron beam is commonly around 70 electron volts. According to the section, about how many kJ/mol is that?
explanation: The beam energy can be varied but is commonly around 70 electron volts (eV), or 6700 kJ/mol. That is enough to knock a valence electron out of an organic molecule.

prompt: When a high-energy electron knocks a valence electron out of an organic molecule, why is the product called a cation radical?

choices.text: It has lost an electron, so it is positive, and it now has an odd number of electrons
It has gained an electron, so it is negative, and it now has an odd number of electrons
choices.why: The molecule loses an electron, so it becomes positively charged (a cation), not negative.

choices.text: It has gained a proton, so it is positive, and all its electrons are paired
choices.why: The electron beam removes an electron; no proton is added. Losing one electron leaves an odd number, which makes it a radical.

choices.text: It has split into a separate cation and a separate radical
choices.why: That describes fragmentation, which can happen next. The species first formed is one particle that is both positive and odd-electron.

explanation: A high-energy electron dislodges a valence electron from the molecule. The product is a cation because the molecule has lost an electron and now has a positive charge, and a radical because it now has an odd number of electrons.

prompt: Why do most of the cation radicals formed by electron bombardment break apart?

choices.text: Electron bombardment transfers so much energy to them
The magnetic field pulls them apart as they pass through
choices.why: The magnetic field only deflects ions along different paths. The fragmentation comes from the energy of the electron impact.

choices.text: They collide with the detector and shatter
choices.why: They fragment right after they form, before they are sorted and detected.

choices.text: They gain a second electron and become unstable
choices.why: They have lost an electron, not gained one. The large energy transfer is what makes them fall apart.

explanation: Electron bombardment transfers so much energy that most of the cation radicals fragment after formation. They break into smaller pieces, some of which keep the positive charge and some of which are neutral.

prompt: In a magnetic-sector mass spectrometer, what happens to neutral fragments?

choices.text: They pass undeflected and are lost on the walls of the pipe
They are deflected the most and reach the detector first
choices.why: A magnetic field deflects only charged particles. Neutral fragments pass undeflected and never reach the detector.

choices.text: They are recorded by the detector as peaks at m/z = 0
choices.why: Neutral fragments never reach the detector, so they give no peaks at all.

choices.text: They are sorted onto the detector along with the positive ions
choices.why: Only positively charged fragments are sorted onto the detector.

explanation: The fragments flow through a curved pipe in a strong magnetic field. Neutral fragments are not deflected and are lost on the walls of the pipe, but positively charged fragments are sorted by m/z onto a detector, which records them as peaks.

prompt: Why is the m/z value of an ion in a mass spectrum usually equal to the ion's mass?

choices.text: The number of charges, z, on each ion is usually 1
The magnetic field cancels out the ion's charge
choices.why: The charge is what lets the field deflect the ion at all. m/z equals m because z is usually 1.

choices.text: The detector records only neutral fragments
choices.why: Neutral fragments never reach the detector; only positive ions do.

choices.text: Each ion carries a number of charges equal to its mass
choices.why: Then m/z would be 1 for every ion. In fact z is usually 1, so m/z equals the mass.

explanation: Ions are sorted by their mass-to-charge ratio, m/z. Since the number of charges z on each ion is usually 1, the value of m/z for each ion is simply its mass m.

prompt: Ions are sorted by their mass-to-charge ratio. If an ion of mass 86 carried two positive charges (z = 2) instead of the usual one, at what m/z value would it appear?
explanation: m/z = 86/2 = 43. Usually z = 1, which is why m/z normally equals the ion's mass; with two charges the ratio is halved.

prompt: Up to approximately how many atomic mass units can an electron-impact, magnetic-sector mass spectrometer analyze?
explanation: Masses up to approximately 2500 atomic mass units (amu) can be analyzed by this type of instrument.

prompt: How does a quadrupole mass analyzer sort ions?

choices.text: For a given field between its four rods, only ions of one m/z get through
A magnetic field bends ions of each m/z onto a different curved path
choices.why: That is the magnetic-sector instrument. A quadrupole uses four parallel rods with an oscillating electrostatic field between them.

choices.text: Its four rods trap the light ions and let all the heavy ions through
choices.why: It isn't a light/heavy split. For a given field, only one m/z value makes it through; all other ions crash into the rods or walls.

choices.text: Its four rods give each passing ion a different number of charges
choices.why: The ions are charged in the ionization source. The quadrupole's field filters them by m/z.

explanation: A quadrupole mass analyzer has four solid rods parallel to the ion beam, with an oscillating electrostatic field between them. For a given field, only one m/z value makes it through; the other ions crash into the rods or walls and never reach the detector.

prompt: In a mass spectrum, what is the base peak?

choices.text: The tallest peak, assigned an intensity of 100%
The peak from the unfragmented cation radical
choices.why: That is the parent peak, or molecular ion. It is often not the tallest peak.

choices.text: The peak at the highest m/z value in the spectrum
choices.why: The base peak is defined by its height, not its position.

choices.text: The peak at the lowest m/z value
choices.why: Position doesn't define it. The base peak is the tallest peak in the spectrum.

explanation: The tallest peak, assigned an intensity of 100%, is called the base peak. The peak for the unfragmented cation radical is the parent peak, or molecular ion (M^+), and it is often not the base peak.

prompt: What does the molecular ion (M^+) peak in a mass spectrum correspond to?

choices.text: The unfragmented cation radical
The tallest peak in the spectrum
choices.why: That is the base peak. The molecular ion is often not the base peak.

choices.text: The neutral molecule before it is ionized
choices.why: Neutral species are never detected. M^+ is the whole molecule after it has lost one electron.

choices.text: The largest fragment left after a methyl group is lost
choices.why: A fragment that has lost a methyl group is lighter than M^+. The molecular ion has not fragmented at all.

explanation: The peak that corresponds to the unfragmented cation radical is called the parent peak, or the molecular ion (M^+, or simply M).

prompt: How is a mass spectrum usually presented?

choices.text: As a bar graph of relative abundance (y axis) against m/z (x axis)
As a bar graph of m/z (y axis) against relative abundance (x axis)
choices.why: The axes are the other way round: m/z values go on the x axis and relative abundance on the y axis.

choices.text: As a bar graph of relative abundance against the ions' charge, z
choices.why: The x axis is the mass-to-charge ratio, m/z, not the charge alone.

choices.text: As a smooth curve of intensity against wavelength
choices.why: A mass spectrum is a bar graph, with one bar for the abundance of ions at each m/z value.

explanation: A mass spectrum is typically a bar graph with masses (m/z values) on the x axis and intensity, the relative abundance of ions of a given m/z striking the detector, on the y axis.

prompt: In the mass spectrum of propane, the molecular ion at m/z = 44 is only about what percentage as high as the base peak at m/z = 29?
explanation: Propane's molecular ion at m/z = 44 is only about 30% as high as the base peak at m/z = 29. Fragmentation patterns are usually complex, and the molecular ion is often not the base peak.
